claims.text: Traditional EAM references are unable to represent the many atomic configurations encountered in an ab initio high-temperature liquid.
Replacing an EAM reference with a deep neural-network interatomic potential trained on high-temperature ab initio data will improve reference–target phase-space overlap.
The proposed potential should be trained across a broad set of solid and liquid atomic configurations obtained from ab initio calculations.
The proposed deep neural-network potential captures many-body interactions.
The machine-learned potential will interpolate the ab initio potential-energy surface more reliably than EAM across diverse atomic configurations.
More reliable interpolation of the ab initio potential-energy surface will reduce mismatch between reference and target phase spaces during thermodynamic integration.
Reduced reference–target phase-space mismatch will decrease thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
Reduced path mismatch will improve the fidelity of computed free energies.
The proposed potential will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by an estimated 40–50% relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The proposed potential will produce free-energy estimates closer to direct ab initio results than those obtained using EAM references.
The intervention applies to both solid and liquid multicomponent high-entropy alloys at and near their melting temperatures.
Configurational diversity is higher in the liquid state than in the solid state.
The intervention will be most effective in systems with highly diverse atomic configurations near melting.
The advantage of the machine-learned reference may be smaller in alloys with less configurational variability or in ordered phases.
The magnitude of path-mismatch reduction depends on training-data quality and coverage, alloy composition, and temperature.
Failure to reduce path mismatch by at least approximately 20% relative to the EAM reference is designated as a falsifying outcome.
Failure of the machine-learned-reference free energy to converge more closely to a direct ab initio benchmark than the EAM-reference result is designated as a falsifying outcome.
